what: NASA says / we get: published NASA values next to the numbers this site uses or produces.

rows.topic: Saffire-III airflow in the flow duct
rows.ours: NASA's PSI-100 record says 30 cm/s, which we used to quote. We now show both. Our smoke model (M3) models the cargo ship's cabin, not the duct, so this number does not enter it.
rows.verdict: Conflict between NASA sources: shown, not hidden
sources: PSI-100 record (30 cm/s, likely the planned value)

rows.topic: How sure are the alarm times? (threshold choice)
rows.nasa: NASA published no alarm times for Saffire-III, so there is nothing to match.
rows.ours: Changing our rule from 4 to 6 standard deviations leaves the flame sensor at 7 s in both burns and moves the smoke detector between 81.5 and 126.5 s. Smoke readings come every ~10 s, so smoke times are +/- 10 s.
rows.verdict: Robust to the threshold (except the loosest, 3 SD)

rows.topic: Does the station's smoke detector miss fine smoke?
rows.nasa: The ISS smoke detector frequently failed to detect the smaller smoke particles from Teflon and Kapton (NIST summary of Meyer et al. 2018; the paper's exact fractions were not checked by us).
rows.ours: Our size-based view agrees in direction: Kapton and Teflon make the finest smoke (42 and 81 nm geometric mean diameter).
sources: Meyer et al., Fire Safety Journal 98:74-81 (2018)

rows.nasa: Kapton unaged average size 0.042 µm; Teflon 0.081 µm (Table 1)

rows.topic: Textbook flame-spread formula on BASS-II slabs
rows.nasa: BASS-II measured spread rates over thin and thick acrylic slabs (summary report, Table 5.1).
rows.ours: The plain de Ris formula over-predicts them: median 3.5-fold, geometric mean 4.4-fold (M6). M6b calibrates it, but a simple lookup by thickness and sides burning does as well or better (see the baselines on the model cards).
sources: Olson et al., BASS-II Summary Report, NASA/TM-20210011385

rows.topic: Lowest oxygen for flame spread over acrylic
rows.nasa: Steady spread seen at 13.6% O2 on rods in BASS-II; opposed spread not seen below 16.4% O2 in other tests.
rows.ours: M6b's calibrated cells for acrylic slabs start at 18% O2 (1 mm: 18-19%; 5 mm: 18-22%); anything lower is labelled outside NASA's data.
rows.verdict: Consistent: low-oxygen cells are not claimed

rows.nasa: About 12% O2 for methanol and 15% for heptane (in nitrogen).
rows.ours: At 12% O2 our model gives at least a 99.9% chance the flame goes out early for every case in its table. Its 50% point (about 20-27% O2) is higher because it predicts going out before the fuel is used up, a stricter question than whether it burns at all.
sources: Dietrich et al. 2014, Microgravity Sci. Technol. 26:65-76

rows.nasa: In CFI-G, cool diffusion flames of gas fuels were seen only in the 2 bar tests, not at lower pressure.
rows.ours: Our cool-flame model's 50% point is at 3.22 atm, and a pressure-only rule (AUC 0.78) almost matches it (0.82): pressure is the main gate.
rows.verdict: Consistent; our model does not yet beat pressure gating
sources: Kim et al., Proc. Combust. Inst. 39 (2023)

rows.topic: Smoke alarm after the gas (Saffire VI)
rows.nasa: Far-field smoke monitor reached 1 mg/m³ at 981 s, after much of the hazardous gas had been released. No time zero is given.
rows.ours: We quote it as reported and do not turn it into a delay. It is a different vehicle and threshold from our Saffire-III times.
